hypotheses.claim: ORM hydration of Invoice entities dominates per‑row cost
hypotheses.mechanism: JpaRepository.findByStatusOnly returns Invoice entities; for each row JPA creates a managed entity, populates all fields and tracks it in the persistence context, which costs ~0.1 ms per row
evidence: Latency per result row is ~0.1 ms for 50 and 100 rows (probe size=50: p50 latency 6.7 ms, rows 50; probe size=100: p50 latency 6.9 ms, rows 100)
Server‑side SQL time drops to 0.3 ms (4 % of latency) for 50/100 rows, so the extra ~1.6 ms when moving from 10→100 rows is not SQL
Response body size grows linearly (53 bytes per row) while latency grows only ~1.6 ms, consistent with a per‑row object‑creation cost
hypotheses.prediction: If the query is changed to return a projection (e.g., interface‑based DTO) instead of full Invoice entities, the p50 latency for 100 rows will drop by >1 ms

hypotheses.claim: JSON serialization of the response adds a modest per‑byte cost
hypotheses.mechanism: Spring MVC uses MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter; each byte of the JSON payload incurs processing (character encoding, buffer allocation) adding ~0.0003 ms per byte
evidence: Response body size is 53 bytes per row (probe size=100: 5384 bytes, size=50: 2674 bytes)
Latency grows roughly proportionally with body size (5.3 ms → 6.9 ms when body grows from 533 B to 5384 B)
The increase (~1.6 ms) exceeds the per‑row ORM cost estimate, indicating a cost that scales with total bytes
hypotheses.prediction: If the endpoint returns a gzipped response (Content‑Encoding: gzip) the measured latency for 100 rows will decrease by at least 0.8 ms

hypotheses.claim: Fixed controller/service overhead (request handling, paging calculation) consumes the bulk of the baseline latency
hypotheses.mechanism: PaidInvoiceSummaryController builds the PageRequest, PaidInvoiceSummaryService computes paging bounds and invokes the repository; Spring MVC resolves the handler, creates ModelAndView, and builds the ResponseEntity – all of which happen once per request and cost ~2 ms
evidence: Even with zero rows (page size 0, not measured but can be inferred) the latency would still be around 5 ms because the p50 for 10 rows is 5.3 ms while per‑row cost is only ~0.1 ms
Application SQL time is only 0.3 ms for large pages, leaving >5 ms unexplained
The call chain (controller → service → repository) executes only one method before the query, suggesting constant‑time work
hypotheses.prediction: If the endpoint is called via MockMvc without the full HTTP stack (bypassing network and servlet filters), the measured p50 latency will drop by at least 1.5 ms

probes_run.result: Latency 5.3 ms, rows 10, SQL 1.6 ms, body 533 B – shows low per‑row cost and a fixed base component.
Latency 6.9 ms, rows 100, SQL 0.3 ms, body 5384 B – latency grows modestly with rows and body size, separating per‑row ORM cost from serialization cost.
